segments.text: Kodak invented one of the world's first digital cameras. Yet decades later, the company that helped create the future of photography filed for bankruptcy.
For decades, Kodak was a giant in photography. People bought its cameras, film rolls, and printing services. Its business was built around capturing memories on film.
Then, in 1975, Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built a digital camera prototype. It was bulky, captured tiny black-and-white images, and took 23 seconds to record a photograph.
But digital photography challenged the economics of Kodak's established film business. The company had to navigate a difficult transition while protecting an enormous existing business.
Kodak tried multiple strategies, but its financial and competitive pressures continued. In January 2012, the company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.
The lesson isn't that Kodak never innovated. It did. The deeper problem was turning innovation into a sustainable business model before the market moved beyond its traditional strengths.
Because inventing the future is one thing. Building a business that can survive it is another.
